passage: I'm Wasim, and I live next door to Suraj, so I hear things through the wall. Last Sunday Suraj's father said, quite loudly, "Who will carry these customs after us?" Suraj's mother looked close to tears. Suraj didn't argue. Suraj said, "I hear you. I'm still coming to the festival dinner and helping with the lamps, I just can't say the words the way I used to." Then I saw Suraj carry the lamps to the courtyard and stand with the family, quiet. I can't tell what Suraj really feels: maybe sad, maybe relieved. Later Suraj's father passed Suraj the sweets. Nobody said much, but it wasn't a fight.

qa.q: What did Suraj's father ask loudly?
qa.a: Suraj's father asked, "Who will carry these customs after us?"

qa.q: What might Suraj be feeling, and why is Wasim unsure?
qa.a: Suraj may be sad or relieved; Wasim only sees behaviour, such as the quiet and the lamps, not the inner state.

qa.q: What could Suraj do in the months ahead?
qa.a: Keep hearing the parents' fear, keep joining the family events that can be joined honestly, and let time do its work.

qa.q: How does Suraj's father see the situation?
qa.a: With fear that the family's traditions may not be passed on, which is why he asks who will carry them.

grounding: Suraj's parents fear the traditions will not be passed on; Suraj hears them and stays part of family events honestly.

passage:
Kishore had stopped going to the temple with his mother around the time he turned sixteen. He hadn't made a speech about it. He just kept saying he had tuition.

On Ganesh Chaturthi morning, in their Pune flat, Rekha was making modaks and not speaking to him. When he came into the kitchen, she said, without turning, "Your grandfather made these with me. I thought one day you'd make them with your children. Now I don't know if there will be anything to pass on."

Kishore stood still. He had thought she was angry. She was afraid.

"Aai," he said, "I don't know what I believe. But I'm not leaving you. I can still make modaks. I can do the decorations with Ajoba's old moulds. I'll be there for the aarti with the family, even if I just stand."

She kept folding the dough. "You'll really help?"

He washed his hands and sat beside her. His first modak split open. She laughed and showed him again.

qa.q: What was Rekha making on Ganesh Chaturthi morning?
What did Kishore realise about his mother's silence?
qa.a: Kishore realised she was not angry but afraid of losing the traditions she wanted to pass on.

qa.q: What did Kishore offer that was honest and kind?
qa.a: Kishore offered to make modaks, do the decorations and stand with the family at aarti, joining in what he honestly could.

qa.q: How does Rekha seem to feel when Kishore sits beside her?
qa.a: Rekha seems relieved and warmed, laughing and showing him how to fold the modak again.

grounding: It shows a teen whose parent fears he is leaving the faith and losing their traditions, who hears her fear and joins family events he can take part in honestly.

passage:
"Indu, you didn't come for the Friday puja again." Amma was folding clothes, not looking up.

"I had a test, Amma."

"You had a test last Friday too." Amma put the sari down. "Gargi said you told her you don't believe in any of it anymore."

Indu glared at her elder sister, who was suddenly very busy with her phone.

"I don't know what I believe," Indu said carefully.

Amma's voice shook. "My mother taught me every song. I taught you both. If you stop, who will sing them after me?"

Indu hadn't thought of it like that. Not as losing God. As losing Amma's songs.

"Amma, I still like the songs. I can learn them properly. I'll help you with the kolam for Pongal, like always. I just can't pretend to pray."

Amma looked at her for a long moment. "Sing with me on Friday, then. Just sing."

"Okay. Just sing."

Gargi looked up and smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Gargi tell Amma about Indu?
qa.a: Gargi said Indu had told her she doesn't believe in any of it anymore.
Amma was afraid that if Indu stopped, the songs her own mother taught her would not be passed on.

qa.q: What did Indu do that was wise?
qa.a: Indu heard Amma's fear, offered to learn the songs and help with the kolam, and was honest that she could not pretend to pray.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel at the end of the conversation?
qa.a: Gargi likely feels relieved that the talk went gently, and perhaps less guilty for telling Amma.

grounding: It shows a teen whose parent fears she is leaving the faith and losing their traditions, who hears the fear and stays part of the family events she can join honestly.
